checking-special-cases-first.label: Checking Special Cases First
checking-special-cases-first.summary: Put invalid, sentinel, or narrower cases before broader cases when that prevents them from being hidden or makes the remaining logic clearer.

sketch1.title: Put specific checks before broad checks

sc-special-before-general.title: Choose the best ordering
sc-special-before-general.prompt: Why is it usually better to check a special case before a broad case in an `if` / `elif` chain?
sc-special-before-general.hint: A first matching branch prevents later branches in the same chain from running.

help.concept: When a broad condition also includes a special value, placing the broad condition first can hide the special branch.
help.hint_1: Ask whether the special value satisfies both conditions.
help.hint_2: If it does, the narrower condition should be checked first.

options.a: Because Python runs every matching branch in order
options.b: Because a broad condition placed first can prevent the special case from being reached
options.d: Because special cases must always be written in `else`

special-cases-come-first.title: Handle invalid or exceptional input early
special-cases-come-first.bodyMarkdown:
Some values should be separated before normal processing begins.

For example, a negative age is invalid:

```python
age = -3

if age < 0:
    print("Invalid")
elif age < 13:
    print("Child")
else:
    print("Older")
```

Python checks the invalid case first.

That gives the rest of the chain a simpler assumption: once execution reaches the second branch, the age is already known to be nonnegative.

Examples:

- `-3` → `Invalid`
- `8` → `Child`
- `20` → `Older`

This is a **validation-first** pattern. The invalid condition does not have to overlap every later condition; handling it early keeps bad input out of the normal cases.

broad-vs-specific.title: Put a narrower matching case before a broader one
broad-vs-specific.bodyMarkdown:
Order becomes essential when one value can satisfy more than one condition.

Consider a perfect score:

```python
score = 100

if score >= 60:
    print("Pass")
elif score == 100:
    print("Perfect")
else:
    print("Fail")
```

The output is:

```text
Pass
```

`100` satisfies both `score >= 60` and `score == 100`, but Python stops at the first true branch.

To preserve the special result, put the narrower condition first:

```python
score = 100

if score == 100:
    print("Perfect")
elif score >= 60:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")
```

Now:

- `100` → `Perfect`
- `75` → `Pass`
- `40` → `Fail`

When conditions overlap, ask which rule matches fewer values. That narrower rule usually belongs first.

using-elif-for-clear-branches.title: Separate sentinel values before normal text
using-elif-for-clear-branches.bodyMarkdown:
A special value can also act as a **sentinel**: a value with a distinct meaning that should be handled separately.

For text input, the empty string can mean “nothing was entered”:

```python
text = input()

if text == "":
    print("Empty")
elif text == "yes":
    print("Confirmed")
else:
    print("Other")
```

These cases do not overlap, so putting the empty string first is not required to prevent `"yes"` from being hidden.

It is still useful because it separates the sentinel case from normal text handling immediately:

1. no text entered;
2. one recognized value;
3. every other text value.

That makes the intent of the chain easier to read and extend later.
